title: Anthem
name: Anthem
metaDescription: Anthem 1031 exchange advisory for owners of Anthem Way community retail, I-17 outlet-corridor pads, and HOA-governed commercial parcels in far north Phoenix.

sections.html: Anthem sits along I-17 in unincorporated Maricopa County north of Phoenix proper, built as a large master-planned community rather than as its own incorporated city. Commercial development is concentrated tightly around the Anthem Way interchange, split between retail serving the community itself and highway-facing retail catching drivers headed north toward Flagstaff and Sedona. An owner exchanging here is buying into a well-defined node, not a spread-out submarket.

sections.heading: Two Different Customers, Two Different Retail Types
sections.html:
Grocery-anchored centers along Anthem Way serve the community's own rooftops, with steady but unspectacular traffic tied to daily errands rather than destination shopping. A short distance away, the outlet retail near the I-17 interchange draws almost entirely from through-traffic headed to or from northern Arizona, and its performance tracks highway volume and tourist season more than anything happening inside Anthem itself. Medical and dental office rounds out most of the rest of the commercial stock, sized to the community rather than to a regional draw.

Weekend and holiday traffic on I-17 headed toward Flagstaff or the Grand Canyon can noticeably boost outlet-corridor sales on a handful of peak days each year, and a buyer should ask for daily sales breakdowns rather than a monthly average when evaluating a tenant in that category.

sections.heading: Where Replacement Capital Usually Goes
sections.html:
Owners exchanging into Anthem commonly consider:

  • Grocery-anchored retail centers along Anthem Way
  • Outlet and highway-facing retail pads near the I-17 interchange
  • Medical and dental office serving the resident base
  • HOA-governed neighborhood commercial parcels
  • Small flex or office space near the interstate frontage

sections.heading: Zoning Runs Through the County, Governance Through the HOA
sections.html:
Because Anthem isn't its own incorporated city, zoning and permitting on any commercial parcel here run through Maricopa County rather than a city planning department, which surprises some buyers used to dealing with an incorporated municipality. On top of that county-level zoning, the Anthem Community Council enforces its own architectural and use standards through recorded CC&Rs, and a buyer should review those documents directly rather than assume county approval alone clears a project.

Signage in particular gets more scrutiny in Anthem than in most incorporated West Valley cities, since both the county sign code and the Community Council's own architectural standards apply, and a tenant improvement plan that would clear easily elsewhere in the Valley can still need a separate round of Community Council sign-off here.

sections.heading: Separating Highway Traffic From Local Traffic in the Underwriting
sections.html: A buyer looking at the outlet or highway-facing retail near the I-17 interchange should underwrite off actual highway traffic counts and seasonal tourist patterns, not off Anthem's resident population, since that category's performance has little to do with how many people live nearby. A buyer looking at the community-serving retail along Anthem Way should do the opposite and focus on rooftop counts and household income inside the community itself.

sections.heading: A Small, Well-Defined Node With Limited Turnover
sections.html: Because the commercial footprint in Anthem is so tightly concentrated around one interchange, the total number of buildings that could serve as a replacement property stays small at any given time. An owner should start working with a broker who already knows the CC&R requirements and the split between highway and local retail well before the relinquished sale closes, since sorting that out after the identification window opens costs time the exchange doesn't have to spare. A broker with existing relationships inside the Anthem Community Council can also shorten how long CC&R review takes once a candidate property is identified.

faqs.q: Is Anthem its own city with its own zoning department?
faqs.a: No. Anthem is unincorporated Maricopa County land, so zoning and permitting on commercial parcels run through the county rather than through a city planning department, which can surprise a buyer used to working with an incorporated municipality.

faqs.q: Do CC&Rs affect commercial property in Anthem as well as homes?
faqs.a: Yes. The Anthem Community Council enforces architectural and use standards through recorded CC&Rs that apply to commercial parcels as well, so review those documents alongside county zoning.

faqs.q: Should I underwrite the outlet retail near I-17 the same way as the community retail on Anthem Way?
faqs.a: No. The I-17 outlet and highway-facing retail tracks highway traffic and tourist season, while the Anthem Way retail tracks the community's own rooftops and household income. Use the right driver for each rather than blending the two into a single set of assumptions.

faqs.q: Does seasonal travel on I-17 really move the needle for outlet-corridor tenants?
faqs.a: It can, noticeably. Weekend and holiday traffic headed to northern Arizona can lift sales on peak days well above the average, so ask for daily sales data rather than relying on a monthly figure.

faqs.q: Can 1031 Exchange of Phoenix confirm whether my Anthem purchase qualifies for a 1031 exchange?
faqs.a: No. That determination belongs to the investor's qualified intermediary, CPA, or tax attorney. This service coordinates sourcing, timelines, and communication among those advisors, working directly alongside the investor's own tax and legal counsel throughout.

faqs.q: Is getting new signage approved harder in Anthem than in other Valley cities?
faqs.a: It can take an extra step. Both the county sign code and the Anthem Community Council's own architectural standards apply, so a tenant improvement plan may need separate Community Council sign-off even after county approval, and building that extra review time into a lease-up timeline is worth doing up front rather than assuming a single approval covers both sets of requirements.
